claims.text: Ab initio two-phase coexistence molecular dynamics can accurately predict a material's melting temperature.
The method can determine the enthalpy of fusion.
The method can determine the entropy of fusion.
The method can determine the volume change at melting.
Two-phase coexistence avoids the high computational cost of full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The solid and liquid regions are allowed to equilibrate during the two-phase simulation.
A sufficiently large simulation cell minimizes solid-liquid interfacial effects.
The stability and dynamics of the solid-liquid interface mediate the phase transition and permit identification of equilibrium conditions.
The temperature at which neither the solid nor the liquid grows at the expense of the other is the melting temperature.
Energy differences between the solid and liquid phases can be used to obtain the enthalpy of fusion.
Coexistence calculations can provide the entropy of fusion.
Volume differences between the solid and liquid phases yield the volume change upon melting.
The predicted fusion properties will agree within uncertainty with results from full ab initio free-energy integration.
The method is reliable when solid-liquid interfacial dynamics are well behaved and the simulation cell is large enough to reduce finite-size effects.
Extremely sluggish kinetics can introduce additional uncertainty into two-phase coexistence results.
Very small simulation cells can introduce additional uncertainty into two-phase coexistence results.
Quantitative accuracy depends on the material system and simulation parameters.
